messages.content: I want to develop a shared-control robot for collaborative object transport. The central challenge is distinguishing a human partner’s change in intent from a correction the person makes in reaction to the robot’s own assistance.

That distinction is central to the goal. During collaborative transport, a human response to the robot’s assistance should not automatically be interpreted as a new intent. At the same time, an actual change in human intent should not be dismissed merely because the robot was assisting. The aim is to distinguish those two possibilities, not to treat every human correction the same way.
Why is the robot’s own assistance important to the wording?

Because the requirement specifically covers cases where the assistance itself induces human corrections. The robot’s action can be part of the situation the human is responding to. That makes an observed correction ambiguous: it may reflect a change in what the person wants to do, or it may be a response to the assistance they are experiencing.
So a correction can be real human behavior without necessarily being a change of intent?

Exactly. Calling it a reaction to assistance does not mean the movement is unreal or should be ignored. It means the movement alone does not settle whether the person has changed their intended course. The distinction concerns what the behavior signifies for shared control.
What is the specific intent-recognition target?

The target is an intent-change F1 score of at least 0.85 for unseen partners, including the condition in which robot assistance itself induces human corrections. It is a stated performance requirement, not a claim that the robot has already achieved it.
Does “unseen partners” matter, or is 0.85 the only important part?

It matters. The threshold is not stated merely for people the system has already encountered. The requirement calls for intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners. The node does not specify a particular way of defining or testing that unfamiliarity, so the important point here is to retain the condition rather than silently drop it.
Could I describe F1 as an accuracy requirement?

It is better to name F1 explicitly. F1 combines precision and recall for the intent-change distinction; it is not simply the fraction of all judgments that are correct. An F1 threshold of 0.85 also does not, by itself, say that precision and recall must each be at least 0.85.
And the robot-induced corrections must be included when interpreting that threshold?

Yes. The target is intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners when the robot’s assistance itself induces human corrections. Leaving out that condition would make the target less specific than the stated requirement. It is precisely the ambiguity created by assistance-induced corrections that the goal calls out.
There is also a control requirement. How should I express it without conflating it with F1?

Express it as a separate outcome: reduce unnecessary control overrides by 30% versus a fixed-assistance baseline, without increasing peak interaction forces. The F1 threshold concerns distinguishing intent changes; the override and force requirements concern how the shared-control interaction performs against the stated baseline.
Is the 30% a percentage-point change?

No. The wording is a 30% reduction versus the fixed-assistance baseline. If the baseline level of unnecessary overrides is represented by B, a 30% reduction would mean a level of 0.70B or lower on the same measure. That illustrates the comparison; it does not supply a baseline value or an observed result.
Does the requirement say to reduce every kind of override?

It specifically says unnecessary control overrides. It does not say that all overrides are undesirable, nor does it provide a detailed rule for classifying an override as unnecessary. Keeping that qualifier is important: removing it would change the target.
Could we meet the override target even if peak interaction forces go up?

Not under the stated requirement. The 30% reduction is coupled with not increasing peak interaction forces. A reduction in unnecessary overrides would not, on its own, satisfy the full control requirement if peak interaction forces increased in that comparison.
Why say peak interaction forces rather than just forces?

Because the requirement is specifically about the peak: the highest interaction forces, rather than a general statement that every force value or an average force must fall. It is important not to replace that condition with a different force measure. The node does not provide a numerical force limit; it says peak interaction forces must not increase.
Would it be fair to say the two numerical targets need to be considered together?

Yes. The goal includes both intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners under assistance-induced corrections and a 30% reduction in unnecessary control overrides versus fixed assistance without increasing peak interaction forces. Meeting one target should not be presented as meeting the other. They describe different aspects of the same shared-control goal.
I also do not want to imply that the robot should always follow a human correction or always oppose it.

That is consistent with the goal. Neither blanket response captures the distinction you want the robot to make. The point is to avoid equating every correction caused by assistance with a changed intent, while remaining able to recognize genuine intent changes. The stated targets do not prescribe a particular control rule for each case.
Can we state the whole goal in one sentence while preserving the conditions?

Develop a shared-control robot for collaborative object transport that distinguishes human intent changes from reactions to its own assistance, achieves intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners when that assistance induces human corrections, and reduces unnecessary control overrides by 30% versus a fixed-assistance baseline without increasing peak interaction forces.
That keeps it as a development goal rather than claiming those results already exist, correct?

Correct. The sentence states what the robot is intended to achieve. It does not claim an experiment has been run, that either numerical target has been met, or that a particular implementation has been chosen.

For the shared-control robot, I propose training partner-invariant, robot-action-conditioned forecasts of human responses. Then it would classify persistent motion that those forecasts do not explain as an intent change, and gate control overrides subject to a peak-interaction-force constraint.

That gives the goal a proposed decision path: account for how the human may respond to the robot’s own action, look for motion that remains unexplained, and use the resulting intent-change classification to gate control overrides. The peak-force constraint remains part of the override decision. This is a proposal for how to approach the goal, not an assertion that the forecasts or classifications already perform as required.
What does “robot-action-conditioned” contribute here?

It means the human-response forecast is made in light of the robot’s action. That matters because a human correction may be a reaction to assistance rather than a change in intent. A forecast that accounts for the robot’s action gives that reaction a place in the interpretation, instead of treating the human motion as if the robot had not influenced it.
Does that mean any response following an action by the robot is explained away?

No. Conditioning on the robot’s action is not the same as declaring every subsequent human motion to be a reaction to it. The proposal calls for comparing the human response with what the forecast can explain. Motion that remains persistently unexplained is the proposed basis for classifying an intent change.
And why specify partner-invariant forecasts?

The aim is for the forecast to capture a useful relationship between robot actions and human responses without depending on the identity of a particular partner. That is especially relevant to the goal’s requirement concerning unseen partners. “Partner-invariant” describes the intended character of the trained forecasts; it does not establish that they will generalize successfully.
So partner-invariant does not mean that every person responds identically?

Right. It does not require identical human behavior. It says the forecasting approach is intended not to rely on partner-specific identity to make the distinction. The proposal leaves open how much responses differ across people and how well the trained forecasts can handle those differences.
What exactly counts as “unexplained motion” in this proposal?

At the conceptual level, it is observed human motion that the robot-action-conditioned human-response forecast does not adequately account for. The proposal does not specify a particular measure of disagreement, a numerical cutoff, or an observation window. Those details should not be treated as settled by the wording.
Is a single unexplained movement enough to classify an intent change?

Not as the proposal is phrased. It calls for *persistent* unexplained motion. That qualifier distinguishes a continuing mismatch from an isolated departure from the forecast. The proposal does not specify how long the mismatch must persist, so it would be premature to assign a duration.
I want to avoid saying the forecast directly reads the human’s intent.

That is a useful distinction. The forecast concerns human responses conditioned on robot actions. The intent-change classification is a subsequent interpretation of persistent motion that remains unexplained by those forecasts. Forecasting a response and determining intent are connected here, but they are not the same operation.
Would it be accurate to describe this as checking whether assistance accounts for a correction before labeling it an intent change?

Yes, as a conceptual description. The robot-action-conditioned forecast is intended to help account for responses to assistance, so a correction is not automatically labeled an intent change. If motion remains persistently unexplained, the proposal treats that as the basis for an intent-change classification. That description does not imply the forecast can establish the cause of every correction with certainty.
Where do control overrides enter the sequence?

After the proposed intent-change classification: the robot uses that classification to gate control overrides. “Gate” means the classification informs whether an override is allowed or called for, rather than making an override automatic whenever there is human motion. The proposal does not specify a detailed override rule.
Does classifying an intent change necessarily require an override?

The proposal does not say that every intent-change classification must trigger one. It says to gate overrides using that classification, with a peak-force constraint. The distinction matters because an intent assessment and an actual control override are separate decisions in the proposed approach.
And the peak-force constraint applies even if the classification suggests an override?

Yes. The wording is to gate *peak-force-constrained* control overrides. The classification does not remove the force constraint. This aligns with the goal of reducing unnecessary overrides versus a fixed-assistance baseline without increasing peak interaction forces, but the proposal alone does not demonstrate either outcome.
Can I say this design will deliver the required intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners?

Not on the basis of the proposal alone. Partner-invariant forecasts and robot-action conditioning are proposed ways to address the difficult case in which assistance induces human corrections. Whether they achieve intent-change F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners remains a performance question, not an established result.
The same caution applies to the 30% reduction in unnecessary overrides, I assume?

Yes. Gating overrides is intended to address unnecessary overrides, but the proposal does not establish a 30% reduction versus the fixed-assistance baseline. Nor does the phrase “peak-force-constrained” itself establish that peak interaction forces will not increase. Those remain requirements against which the proposed approach would have to be assessed.
Could you restate the proposal without adding a particular model or control algorithm?

Train human-response forecasts intended to be partner-invariant and conditioned on the robot’s actions; use persistent motion that those forecasts cannot explain to classify an intent change; then use that classification to gate control overrides while constraining peak interaction forces. That retains the proposed sequence without specifying a model architecture, a persistence threshold, or a detailed override policy.
So the forecast is meant to prevent the robot from mistaking its own influence on the human for a new human intention?

That is the motivation. By accounting for the robot’s action when forecasting a human response, the proposal gives assistance-induced corrections a way to be understood without immediately counting them as intent changes. Persistent motion left unexplained by that account is then treated differently. It remains a proposed distinction, not a guarantee that every reaction and intent change can be separated.
Can robot-action-conditioned motion forecasts separate assistance-induced corrections from genuine intent changes for unseen partners?

That is the central open question. Conditioning a motion forecast on the robot’s action could help account for corrections made in response to its assistance. If a person’s motion remains unexplained by that account, it may be evidence of an intent change. But the forecast alone does not prove why a person moved, and the question is whether the distinction remains useful for partners the robot has not encountered before.
What would the forecast need to distinguish, conceptually?

It would need to distinguish motion that is consistent with a response to the robot’s assistance from motion that indicates the person wants something different. Both can look like a correction, so observing a correction is not enough. The robot’s action provides context for interpreting it, rather than an automatic label.
If a movement is predicted after a robot action, can we call it assistance-induced?

Not with certainty on that basis alone. A forecast that accounts for the movement shows that it is compatible with the anticipated response to the robot’s action. It does not establish that the robot’s assistance was the person’s only reason for moving, or rule out a genuine intent change that happens to resemble a predicted response.
And if the movement is not predicted, is that a genuine intent change?

Not necessarily. Unexplained motion may support an intent-change interpretation, especially if it persists, but it can also expose a limitation of the forecast. The proposed distinction depends on whether the forecast accounts well enough for assistance-induced responses that an unexplained pattern is informative rather than merely unexpected.
Why does the question emphasize unseen partners?

Because the distinction should not depend on already knowing how one particular person tends to respond. For an unseen partner, the forecast has to remain useful without prior familiarity with that person. A forecast could appear to distinguish the two kinds of motion for familiar partners yet fail to make the same distinction for someone new; the question asks whether it can generalize.
Does robot-action conditioning address that generalization issue by itself?

No. Robot-action conditioning addresses one source of ambiguity: the robot’s own assistance may prompt a human correction. Generalization to unseen partners is a separate challenge. Knowing what the robot did can help interpret a response, but it does not guarantee that the forecast will characterize an unfamiliar person’s response accurately.
How should we interpret “separate” here? Must the two cases have completely different motion?

No. The question is whether the forecasts provide a useful basis for telling the cases apart, not whether the motions are always visibly distinct or can be separated perfectly. Similar-looking motions can have different meanings. Conditioning on the robot’s action may add relevant context, while still leaving some cases ambiguous.
So the question is not simply whether motion can be forecast accurately?

Right. Forecasting motion is a means to the intended distinction. A forecast could describe many human responses well without reliably telling an assistance-induced correction from an intent change. Conversely, the important issue is whether what the forecast explains—and what remains unexplained—helps make that particular distinction for unseen partners.
Is persistence relevant to the question, or only to the proposed classification?

It is relevant as part of the proposed interpretation: persistent unexplained motion would be treated as more suggestive of an intent change than a momentary departure from the forecast. But persistence does not resolve the question by itself. If a forecast systematically fails to account for an unseen partner’s response to assistance, the resulting mismatch could also persist.
Would you answer the question yes or no at this stage?

I would leave it open. The proposal explains why robot-action-conditioned forecasts might help separate the cases, but it supplies no result establishing that they do so for unseen partners. An unconditional yes would claim success that has not been shown; an unconditional no would dismiss a possibility the question is asking us to examine.
Can you phrase the uncertainty without making the idea sound empty?

The idea has a clear rationale: account for motion expected in response to the robot’s assistance before interpreting a correction as a change in intent. The unresolved issue is whether that account is reliable enough for unseen partners that persistent unexplained motion meaningfully indicates a genuine intent change, rather than a forecasting error. That is a substantive question, not a result yet.
I want to keep genuine intent changes from being explained away, too.

Yes—that is the other side of the distinction. If the forecast treats a genuine change as an ordinary response to assistance, it would miss the very event it is meant to recognize. The question therefore asks whether conditioning on the robot’s action helps avoid mistaken intent-change labels without simply absorbing genuine changes into the forecast.
Then the concise version is whether accounting for the robot’s own action makes the human correction interpretable, even when the partner is new?

Yes, provided “interpretable” retains the specific distinction: can the robot-action-conditioned motion forecast help tell a correction induced by assistance from a genuine intent change for an unseen partner? It should remain a question about that distinction, not a claim that accounting for the robot’s action already settles it.

I want to state a testable hypothesis for the distinction we’ve been discussing: with assistance-induced corrections, action-conditioned residuals will achieve unseen-partner intent-change F1 ≥0.85, at least 0.10 above action-blind residuals.

That states two predictions for the same condition. When robot assistance induces human corrections, intent-change classification using action-conditioned residuals is hypothesized to reach F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners. Its F1 is also hypothesized to exceed that of action-blind residuals by at least 0.10. Neither prediction is an observed result.
What does “action-conditioned residuals” mean in this hypothesis?

Conceptually, a residual is the part of observed human motion left unexplained by a motion forecast. An action-conditioned residual comes from a forecast that takes the robot’s action into account. The hypothesis is that those residuals will be more useful for identifying intent changes when the human may also be correcting in response to the robot’s assistance.
And what is the action-blind comparison?

Action-blind residuals come from a forecast that does not condition on the robot’s action. They provide the comparison for the proposed advantage of accounting for what the robot did. The hypothesis does not specify any further difference in how the two sets of residuals are produced.
Why include the action-blind comparison if I already have the F1 target of 0.85?

The two thresholds ask different things. F1 ≥0.85 sets an absolute intent-change performance target for unseen partners under assistance-induced corrections. The margin of at least 0.10 asks whether action conditioning improves F1 over action-blind residuals. Reaching the absolute target alone would not establish the predicted margin.
Could the margin be met without reaching 0.85?

Yes, mathematically, but that would not satisfy the full hypothesis. For example, F1 values of 0.80 and 0.69 would differ by 0.11, yet the action-conditioned value would remain below 0.85. Those numbers are only an illustration of how the two thresholds differ, not reported results.
Could the 0.85 threshold be met without the margin?

Yes. For example, action-conditioned F1 of 0.86 and action-blind F1 of 0.80 would meet the absolute threshold but differ by only 0.06. Again, that is an illustrative calculation, not a finding. The hypothesis requires both F1 ≥0.85 and an advantage of at least 0.10.
Is “at least 0.10 above” a relative percentage improvement?

No. As worded, it is a difference of at least 0.10 in F1 score: action-conditioned F1 minus action-blind F1 must be ≥0.10. It does not say the action-conditioned score must be 10% higher relative to the action-blind score.
If the action-conditioned F1 were exactly 0.85, what would the comparison require?

At exactly 0.85, an advantage of at least 0.10 would require action-blind F1 to be no higher than 0.75. That is a consequence of the stated difference, not a claim that either score has been observed. If the action-conditioned F1 were higher, the corresponding maximum action-blind score would change with it.
I want to be careful about the condition. Is this a general prediction for any human motion?

No. The stated condition is that assistance induces human corrections, and the F1 target is for unseen partners. The hypothesis concerns recognizing intent changes in that setting. It does not assert the same thresholds for every kind of motion or every interaction condition.
Does it claim that all assistance-induced corrections can be separated from intent changes?

No. F1 ≥0.85 is a performance threshold, not a claim of perfect separation. The hypothesis predicts that action-conditioned residuals will support intent-change classification well enough to reach that threshold and outperform action-blind residuals by the stated margin. It leaves open the possibility of individual mistakes.
Does a small action-conditioned residual always mean there was no intent change?

The hypothesis does not establish such a rule. It concerns the F1 of intent-change classification using action-conditioned residuals, not an infallible interpretation of each residual. A motion forecast could account for some movement associated with a genuine change, just as it could fail to account for a response to assistance. Whether the residuals support the predicted distinction is what remains to be determined.
So should I say the hypothesis answers the earlier question?

It proposes a specific, measurable answer: under assistance-induced corrections, accounting for the robot’s action is predicted to yield unseen-partner intent-change F1 ≥0.85 and an F1 advantage of at least 0.10 over action-blind residuals. As a hypothesis, it does not yet establish that the separation works.
Does the hypothesis also predict fewer unnecessary control overrides?

Not explicitly. This hypothesis makes claims about intent-change F1 and the comparison between action-conditioned and action-blind residuals. The shared-control goal also concerns unnecessary overrides and peak interaction forces, but those outcomes should not be presented as consequences already demonstrated—or as additional numerical predictions—by this hypothesis.
Nor does it specify a particular forecast model, correct?

Correct. It names the distinction between action-conditioned and action-blind residuals and gives the two F1 criteria. It does not choose a model architecture, define a particular residual computation, or specify a classification threshold. Adding any of those as settled details would go beyond this hypothesis.
Can you give me a compact version that keeps the comparison unambiguous?

Hypothesis: When robot assistance induces human corrections, intent-change classification using action-conditioned residuals will achieve F1 ≥0.85 for unseen partners, with F1 at least 0.10 higher than classification using action-blind residuals.

To address whether robot-action-conditioned motion forecasts can distinguish assistance-induced corrections from genuine intent changes for unseen partners, I plan to randomize assistance pulses during transport, annotate goal changes, train action-conditioned and action-blind forecasters, and compare unseen-partner intent-change F1.

That plan connects the question to a comparison. The randomized assistance pulses provide variation in what the robot does during transport; the goal-change annotations identify the events the intent-change assessment is meant to recognize. The two forecasters differ in whether they account for the robot’s action, and the comparison is their intent-change F1 for unseen partners. These are planned steps, not completed observations.
Why randomize the assistance pulses rather than simply observe whatever assistance happens during transport?

Randomization makes variation in the robot’s assistance an explicit part of the plan. That is relevant because the question concerns human motion that may be a response to the robot’s own action. It does not, by itself, tell us whether any particular human movement is a correction caused by assistance or a genuine goal change; that distinction remains what the comparison is meant to examine.
Does the plan specify the size or timing of the pulses?

No. It says to randomize assistance pulses during transport, but it does not specify their magnitude, duration, timing, or randomization scheme. Those details should not be treated as already decided.
Is an assistance pulse itself a goal change?

No. In the plan, an assistance pulse is a robot action during transport. A goal change concerns the human partner’s intent. Keeping those concepts separate is essential: the question is whether a human response to assistance can be distinguished from a genuine change in what the person intends.
What role do the goal-change annotations play?

They provide the reference for assessing intent-change identification. Without a way to distinguish annotated goal changes from other motion in the comparison, intent-change F1 would not answer the stated question. The plan calls for annotating goal changes, but it does not specify who annotates them or by what procedure.
Are we also planning to annotate every assistance-induced correction?

That is not stated here. The plan specifically says to annotate goal changes. Assistance-induced corrections motivate the comparison, but the plan does not add a separate correction-annotation scheme or claim that every such correction will receive its own label.
Why train two forecasters?

Training both makes it possible to compare forecasts that account for the robot’s action with forecasts that do not. The action-conditioned forecaster has the robot’s action as context; the action-blind forecaster is the comparison that lacks that conditioning. Their unseen-partner intent-change F1 can then be compared without assuming in advance that either one will be better.
Does action-blind mean it ignores the human’s motion?

No. Both are motion forecasters in this plan. “Action-blind” distinguishes the forecaster that does not condition on the robot’s action; it does not mean disregarding human motion. The plan does not otherwise specify the forecasters’ inputs or designs.
Do the forecasters themselves have to output an intent-change label?

The plan does not specify that. It calls for training forecasters and comparing intent-change F1, so their forecasts must be used in an intent-change assessment somehow. But it leaves the exact connection between forecasts and intent-change judgments unspecified. It would be an added implementation detail to claim that either forecaster directly outputs the label.
Why is the comparison specifically for unseen partners?

Because the question asks whether the distinction works for people not previously encountered by the trained approach. Comparing unseen-partner F1 keeps the evaluation focused on that generalization issue, rather than only asking whether the forecasts work for partners already familiar to them. The plan does not specify how partners will be assigned to training or comparison.
Could the action-conditioned forecaster fit responses to the robot’s pulses well and still fail on intent changes?

Yes. Forecasting human motion and recognizing goal changes are related but distinct. A forecaster might account for responses to assistance without providing a useful distinction when a genuine goal change occurs. That is why the plan compares intent-change F1, rather than treating good-looking motion forecasts alone as the answer.
Could it also mistake unfamiliar responses to assistance for goal changes?

That remains possible, especially for an unseen partner. A response the forecast does not account for is not automatically a goal change. Comparing intent-change judgments with the goal-change annotations is meant to expose that kind of confusion as well as missed changes, without presuming what the outcome will be.
What does F1 tell us in this comparison?

Intent-change F1 summarizes the balance between identifying annotated goal changes and avoiding incorrect intent-change identifications. Comparing the two forecasters’ F1 for unseen partners asks whether conditioning on robot action helps with that distinction. It is not merely a measure of how closely either forecast traces the person’s motion.
Should I say that randomizing the pulses proves which individual corrections were caused by the robot?

No. Randomizing the robot’s assistance is relevant to studying responses to its action, but the plan does not establish the cause of each individual movement. It also does not specify a method for assigning a causal explanation to each correction. The stated assessment is the comparison of unseen-partner intent-change F1 against annotated goal changes.
Is the action-conditioned forecaster necessarily going to have the higher F1?

The plan does not say so. It sets up a comparison that can reveal whether accounting for robot action helps, makes no difference, or performs worse on that measure. Training and comparing the forecasters should not be phrased as if an advantage has already been observed.
Does this plan also test whether control overrides decrease or whether peak interaction forces stay unchanged?

Not as stated. Its specified comparison is unseen-partner intent-change F1 for action-conditioned and action-blind forecasters. It does not include an override comparison or a peak-force assessment, so those outcomes should not be claimed on the basis of this plan.
Can you restate the plan without filling in missing experimental details?

During collaborative transport, randomize the robot’s assistance pulses and annotate human goal changes. Train an action-conditioned motion forecaster and an action-blind motion forecaster, then compare their intent-change F1 for unseen partners. The plan leaves pulse settings, annotation procedures, forecaster implementations, and results unspecified.

So the key test is not whether pulses happen to produce visible corrections, but whether accounting for the robot’s action improves the distinction between responses to assistance and annotated changes of goal for new partners?

Yes. The assistance pulses make the robot’s actions part of the planned transport setting, while the goal-change annotations anchor the intent-change assessment. Comparing unseen-partner intent-change F1 for the action-conditioned and action-blind forecasters addresses whether accounting for robot action helps with that distinction. The comparison has been proposed, not yet answered.

For the collection activity, let’s call it TransportPulse-24: 24 partners carry trays under randomized assistance pulses and cued, annotated destination changes. Six partners are reserved as unseen partners.

TransportPulse-24 names the collection activity and its scope: tray transport with 24 partners, randomized assistance pulses, and destination changes that are cued and annotated. Reserving six partners as unseen preserves a partner-level group for the later unseen-partner comparison. This describes what is to be collected; it does not report that collection or analysis has been completed.
Why include both assistance pulses and destination changes?

They serve different roles in the activity. The randomized pulses vary the robot’s assistance during transport, which can elicit human responses to that assistance. The cued, annotated destination changes provide identifiable changes in the transport goal. Having both in the collection setting is relevant to distinguishing a response to assistance from a change in intent.
Is an assistance-induced correction itself one of the annotated destination changes?

Not by definition. A correction in response to assistance and a destination change are the two kinds of events the broader question asks us to distinguish. TransportPulse-24 explicitly calls for annotating the cued destination changes; it does not say that every assistance-induced correction receives a separate annotation.
What does “cued” add to the description of a destination change?

It says the destination changes are prompted as part of the activity, rather than merely inferred afterward from whatever motion occurs. The description also says those changes are annotated. It does not specify the cue format, who delivers it, or exactly when it occurs.
Should we call these arbitrary changes of human intent?

It is more precise to call them cued destination changes. They provide instances of a changed transport destination, but the activity description does not characterize every possible kind of intent change or say that spontaneous changes are included.
And “randomized assistance pulses” does not mean the destination changes are randomized too, correct?
Correct. Randomization is explicitly attached to the assistance pulses. The destination changes are described as cued and annotated, with no randomization procedure specified for them.
How should I describe the six unseen partners without assuming details of the eventual models?

You can say that six of the 24 partners are reserved as unseen partners for the intended unseen-partner assessment. That states the reservation without claiming a particular training procedure, model architecture, or result. The description does not specify how the six are selected.
Would it be accurate to say the other 18 are definitely the training set?

Twenty-four minus six leaves 18 partners who are not in the reserved unseen group. But the activity does not explicitly assign all 18 to training, or specify any further division among them. Calling all 18 a defined training set would add a detail not stated here.
Does reserving six partners mean reserving six transport trials?
No. The reservation is stated in partners, not trials: six unseen partners. The activity does not specify how many transports or observations each partner contributes.
Why is it important that the reserved group is at the partner level?

Because the question concerns performance for unseen partners. Holding out partners addresses whether the intended distinction carries over to people outside those used to develop the approach. The activity does not yet establish how well it carries over; it simply reserves six partners for that purpose.
Can I say TransportPulse-24 has already demonstrated unseen-partner intent-change F1 ≥0.85?

No. This node specifies a collection activity, not a measured F1 result. The annotations and reserved partners make an unseen-partner intent-change comparison possible in principle, but they do not supply a score or show that any threshold has been reached.
Nor does the activity say the action-conditioned forecaster beats the action-blind one?

Right. TransportPulse-24 specifies the tray-carrying setting, pulses, destination changes, annotations, and partner reservation. It does not report trained forecasters or their comparative performance.
Does it specify how large the pulses are or what assistance setting serves as a baseline?

No. It says the assistance pulses are randomized during tray transport, but gives no pulse magnitude, timing, distribution, or baseline setting. Those should not be filled in as though they were part of the activity description.
Do we know how many destination changes each partner makes?

No. The activity specifies cued, annotated destination changes but not their number per partner, their timing, or the number of transport runs. The fixed quantities given here are 24 partners in total and six reserved unseen partners.
What is the narrowest useful description of what the annotations establish?

They mark the cued destination changes. That gives an explicit reference for those goal-change events in the collected activity. It does not, on its own, establish the cause of every other human motion or classify each response to an assistance pulse.
Could a partner’s reaction to a pulse and a cued destination change both matter during transport?

Yes, the activity includes both kinds of circumstances during tray transport. That is why interpreting human motion can be challenging: robot assistance can prompt a correction, while a destination change calls for recognizing a changed goal. The description does not specify whether, when, or how closely particular pulses and cues coincide.
Please give me a concise activity statement that preserves all the concrete details without claiming a result.

Collect TransportPulse-24 with 24 partners carrying trays under randomized assistance pulses and cued, annotated destination changes, reserving six partners as unseen. This states the collection activity and reservation, without implying that data collection or performance evaluation has already been completed.
The artifact from this activity is the TransportPulse-24 dataset: synchronized human motion, robot commands, interaction forces, and intent-change labels, with an 18-train/6-unseen-partner split.

That specifies both the dataset contents and its partner-level split. TransportPulse-24 brings the human motion, robot commands, interaction forces, and intent-change labels into a synchronized record. Eighteen partners are designated for training and six as unseen partners; the split is by partner, not merely by individual observations.
What is important about calling the records synchronized?

It means the recorded streams can be related in time: human motion can be considered alongside robot commands, interaction forces, and intent-change labels from the same period. That is important when asking whether motion follows assistance or corresponds to a labeled change in intent. The artifact description does not specify a sampling rate or synchronization method.
Do the robot commands tell us what the human intended?

No. They record what the robot was commanded to do, which is relevant context for interpreting the human response. Human intent is represented separately by the intent-change labels. A robot command alone does not establish why a person moved.
And human motion alone is not the label either?

Correct. Human motion is an observed stream, while intent-change labels identify the changes against which an intent-change assessment can be compared. Keeping them distinct avoids treating every correction in motion as a labeled change of intent.
What do the interaction forces add to the artifact?

If recognition lagged behind a genuine change in what the person wanted to do, the person and robot might temporarily act at cross-purposes. So a 29-N peak cannot itself tell us how late the intent estimate was?

Correct. A force peak has a magnitude, but that magnitude does not provide a recognition time. None of those timings is supplied in this question.
If a force peak occurred after a destination change, would that prove the person was pushing back because recognition was delayed?

No. Occurring after a destination change would establish an order of events, not the cause of the force. The proposed explanation also requires evidence of delayed recognition and human counterforce in relation to the peak. Temporal proximity alone would not settle either point.
Could the cap be working as intended and the interaction force still reach 29 N?

That cannot be resolved without knowing exactly what the controller’s 25-N cap limits and what the 29-N measurement includes. The question deliberately puts those values in tension. I don’t want to imply the human is at fault for the high force.

No. The stated value is the reported interaction-force peak of 29 N. It does not say that every interaction, every partner, or every destination change produced a 29-N force.
Should I treat ‘delayed intent recognition’ as something already measured?

Not from this node. It is part of the explanation being questioned. The 29-N peak and the 25-N controller cap are stated; a delay in recognizing intent, and its possible connection to human counterforces, remain to be established.
What would actually distinguish this explanation from merely noticing that the peak exceeded the cap value?

The distinction is between a numerical observation and a causal account. The observation is that interaction force reached 29 N although the controller had a 25-N cap. Without that connection, the proposed mechanism remains a question.

No. An aggregate F1 score concerns intent-change classification across cases. That timing may be relevant, but it is not the only relationship in the question. Can we at least conclude that specifying a 25-N cap was not enough to ensure measured interaction-force peaks stayed at 25 N?

For the reported interaction, yes: the measured peak was 29 N, so the presence of a stated 25-N controller cap did not coincide with a measured peak at or below 25 N. Ask whether the 29-N interaction-force peaks arose from human counterforces while genuine intent changes were recognized late, despite the controller’s 25-N cap. That preserves the observed peak, the cap, and the proposed timing-dependent mechanism while leaving the causal answer open.
I want to make the force-peak explanation testable: force peaks above 25 N coincide with human counterforces during the 300-ms gating delay after destination changes.

That is a hypothesis about the timing of three things: a destination change, human counterforce during the 300-ms gating delay, and an interaction-force peak above 25 N. “Coincide” makes a narrower prediction about when the counterforces and force peaks occur. Even if they overlap, that alone would not establish what produced a peak. Saying “caused by” would turn the proposed temporal association into a stronger claim than this hypothesis states.

It is *above* 25 N. A peak of exactly 25 N would not meet that wording; a peak greater than 25 N would. The hypothesis does not say that every qualifying peak has the same magnitude.

I’d like to propose calibrated dual-hypothesis filtering to distinguish human intent changes from reactions to the robot’s assistance, and to soften robot authority when the distinction is uncertain.

That proposal keeps both interpretations in view: the human may have changed intent, or may be responding to the robot’s assistance. A calibrated filter would aim to make its expressed uncertainty meaningful, and the shared-control response would soften robot authority when it cannot confidently distinguish the two. This is a proposed approach, not an established performance result.
What does “dual-hypothesis” mean here?

It means considering the two competing explanations explicitly rather than treating every human correction as an intent change or every correction as a reaction to assistance. The proposal does not prescribe a particular mathematical filter or say that every observed movement fits neatly into one explanation.
Does the filter have to make a definite choice between them immediately?

Not as proposed. Its uncertainty is consequential: when the distinction is unclear, the robot should soften its authority. Forcing an immediate, confident choice in every case would miss that part of the proposal.
Why is calibration important rather than just producing a confidence number?

Calibration concerns whether stated confidence is trustworthy, not merely whether a number can be produced. If the system expresses high confidence, that expression should be warranted; when the evidence is ambiguous, it should reflect that ambiguity. The proposal calls for calibrated filtering but does not claim calibration has already been achieved or specify how to measure it.
Does calibration guarantee that the filter will identify every genuine intent change?

No. Calibration and correct classification are related but different. A filter can appropriately express uncertainty and still make mistakes; conversely, an occasional correct judgment does not establish that its confidence is calibrated. The proposal does not guarantee perfect recognition.
What exactly is meant by ‘robot authority’?

Here it refers broadly to how strongly the robot asserts its assistance or control in the shared interaction. Softening that authority under uncertainty means being less assertive rather than acting as though an ambiguous interpretation were certain. The proposal does not define a particular control quantity or adjustment rule.
Would softening authority mean releasing all assistance?

Not necessarily. ‘Soften’ does not specify complete release, nor does it specify an amount of reduction. It states the direction of the response under uncertainty without committing to a particular implementation.
Is the robot supposed to soften authority whenever it sees a human correction?

The stated trigger is uncertainty about whether the motion reflects changed intent or a reaction to assistance, not the mere existence of a correction. A correction might be interpreted with greater or lesser confidence; the proposal does not impose the same response on all corrections.
If the person genuinely changes intent, could softening authority interfere with recognizing that?

That is a possibility the approach would need to handle. Softening authority is a control response to uncertainty, not a declaration that the person has *not* changed intent. The filter must still distinguish genuine changes from assistance reactions; the proposal does not say uncertainty should be resolved by ignoring the human.
What if the motion is actually just a reaction to assistance?

Then treating it as a definite new intent could prompt an unwarranted control response. Keeping the reaction hypothesis active helps avoid that premature interpretation. But the proposal does not claim the filter can know the cause of every individual movement.
Could you give a general illustration without defining an algorithm?

Suppose human motion could plausibly reflect either a newly intended direction or an adjustment to the robot’s assistance. A dual-hypothesis filter would keep both explanations in consideration. If the available evidence does not favor one clearly, the robot would respond with softer authority rather than behaving as though the interpretation were settled. That illustrates the proposal, not a prescribed decision rule.
Does ‘calibrated’ mean assigning equal weight to both explanations?

No. Equal weight would be just one possible expression of uncertainty in a particular case. Calibration means that whatever confidence the filter expresses should correspond appropriately to how reliable its judgments are. The proposal supplies no fixed weights or probability formula.
Are these hypotheses claims about the person’s motives?

They are competing interpretations of behavior relevant to shared control: a change in intent versus a response to the robot’s assistance. The filter would not directly observe a person’s private motives. Its judgments and uncertainty would have to be understood as interpretations, not infallible access to intent.
Should I say the robot becomes passive whenever it is uncertain?

That would be stronger than ‘soften robot authority.’ The proposal calls for a less assertive robot response under uncertainty, not necessarily passivity or surrendering all control. It leaves the precise behavior unspecified.
Is there an uncertainty threshold specified?

No. The proposal does not set a numerical confidence threshold, specify how uncertainty is computed, or define how much authority should change at a given uncertainty level. Those details remain open.
Does the proposal prescribe sensors, motion forecasts, or a particular force limit?

No. It names a calibrated dual-hypothesis filtering approach and an uncertainty-dependent change in robot authority. It does not specify sensing hardware, a forecasting architecture, or a numerical force limit. Adding any of those as settled features would go beyond the proposal.
How does this relate to the goal of distinguishing intent changes from assistance reactions during collaborative object transport?

It addresses that distinction directly by treating the two interpretations as alternatives and making ambiguity visible to the shared controller. Softening authority under uncertainty is meant to avoid overly assertive assistance when the interpretation is unsettled. The proposal alone does not establish intent-change F1 or any override or force outcome.
Could the filter’s calibration by itself establish the unseen-partner F1 requirement?

No. An intent-change F1 of at least 0.85 for unseen partners when assistance induces human corrections is a separate performance requirement. Proposing calibrated confidence does not supply an F1 score or show that the filter generalizes to unseen partners.
And does softer authority automatically deliver the required 30% reduction in unnecessary overrides without increasing peak interaction forces?

No. Softening authority is the proposed behavior under uncertainty, not a measured 30% reduction versus fixed assistance or evidence that peak interaction forces do not increase. Those outcomes cannot be assumed from the control idea alone.
Can I describe this as a way of responding to ambiguity rather than concealing it?

Yes. The filter is intended to represent uncertainty between intent change and assistance reaction, and the robot is proposed to moderate its authority when that uncertainty matters. That description preserves the idea without claiming ambiguity has already been resolved.
