Can we claim the differences are statistically significant?
No statistical test or uncertainty estimate is supplied. The result supports reporting the four values as observed outcomes, not a significance claim or a confidence interval.
Does ‘on 12 unseen partners’ establish that the same figures will hold for any new person?

No. It states the group on which these outcomes were reported. There are no partner-by-partner results or grounds here for guaranteeing identical latency, F1, override behavior, or peak force for another partner.
Can I combine F1, latency, overrides, and force into one overall improvement number?

No combination rule is provided, and the outcomes have different meanings and units. The clearest report leaves the 185-ms latency, 0.86 F1, 32% relative override reduction, and 24-N peak force separate.
Give me a concise result sentence with the comparator attached only to its reported measure.
On 12 unseen partners, early release recorded 185-ms destination-change latency, intent-change F1 of 0.86, 32% fewer overrides than fixed assistance, and 24-N peak interaction force.
The controller artifact is EarlyRelease-v1. It integrates 300-ms intent gating, early counterforce-triggered assistance release, partner calibration, and force-limited assistance.

EarlyRelease-v1 is the integrated controller artifact. Its four stated elements are a 300-ms intent gate, assistance release triggered early by counterforce, partner calibration, and force-limited assistance. Describing what the controller integrates does not, by itself, establish how well it performs or say that it has been deployed.
What is the difference between the intent gate and the assistance release?

The 300-ms intent gate concerns the controller’s handling of a possible intent change. Counterforce-triggered release concerns its assistance when counterforce is detected. They are distinct parts of EarlyRelease-v1: releasing assistance need not be described as a completed judgment that the partner changed intent.
Does ‘early’ give us an exact release time?

No. The artifact names early counterforce-triggered release, but does not state a counterforce-to-release time, a numerical trigger threshold, or a detailed sequence of controller events. The only duration specified in its description is the 300-ms intent-gating setting.
Could I say assistance is always released at the start of that 300-ms period?

That would add a timing rule the description does not provide. It is accurate to say EarlyRelease-v1 integrates early release triggered by counterforce alongside 300-ms intent gating, without fixing the release to a particular instant in the gate.
Does the 300 ms tell us how long a partner must apply counterforce?
No. It describes the intent-gating setting, not a required duration of human counterforce. The artifact description does not state how long counterforce must last to trigger release.
What does counterforce establish about the partner’s intention?

By itself, counterforce does not establish that the partner has changed destination or is reacting to assistance. In EarlyRelease-v1 it is named as a trigger for assistance release, while intent gating remains a separate element. The artifact does not claim that opposing force is an infallible intent label.
Is partner calibration another name for the counterforce trigger?

No. Partner calibration concerns adapting the controller to a partner. Counterforce-triggered release names a control response to detected counterforce. EarlyRelease-v1 integrates both, but its description does not specify how calibration affects the trigger or the intent gate.
Does the artifact say what partner information is used for calibration?

No. It states that partner calibration is integrated, without specifying its inputs, procedure, duration, or resulting settings. Those details should not be supplied as though they were part of the artifact description.
Can I call that calibration label-free?

EarlyRelease-v1’s stated content says ‘partner calibration’ but does not explicitly characterize that component as label-free. To describe this artifact on its own terms, use ‘partner calibration’ without adding an unstated input restriction.
And what is meant by force-limited assistance?

It means the assistance is subject to a force limit as part of the controller. The description does not state a limit in newtons, define exactly which force quantity is constrained, or report a measured interaction-force peak. A controller feature and its measured force outcome should be kept distinct.
Could I specify a 25-N cap when naming EarlyRelease-v1?
Not from this artifact description. It identifies force-limited assistance but gives no numerical cap. Adding 25 N as a defined setting of EarlyRelease-v1 would go beyond what is stated here.
Does force-limited assistance mean no interaction force can ever exceed the controller’s limit?

The description does not establish that guarantee. It names a constraint on assistance, not a verified bound on every measured interaction force in every use. It also leaves the limit’s implementation unspecified.
Are force-limited assistance and early release interchangeable ways of describing the same control action?

No. Early release describes a response triggered by counterforce. Force-limited assistance describes a constraint on the assistance the robot provides. Both are integrated in EarlyRelease-v1; neither phrase replaces the other.
Would it be accurate to say the controller coordinates all four elements?

You can say it integrates them. ‘Coordinates’ can be used in that broad sense, but it should not imply a particular ordering, threshold rule, or measured success that the artifact description does not specify.
Does the artifact define how the partner calibration changes the 300-ms gate?

No. It specifies a 300-ms intent gate and partner calibration as components, but does not say calibration changes that duration. Describing a partner-dependent gate length would add a detail not given for EarlyRelease-v1.
Could the intent gate be called a measured 300-ms destination-change latency?

No. The 300 ms is a controller setting. Destination-change latency would be an observed timing outcome, and this artifact description does not report one. Equating the two would misstate what is specified.
What if someone assumes a counterforce-triggered release must wait until the intent gate finishes?

The artifact does not specify that dependency. It expressly includes *early* counterforce-triggered release as well as 300-ms intent gating, so it is better to keep the control response and the intent-gating process distinct rather than claim a prescribed wait or an exact release instant.
Does EarlyRelease-v1 classify every correction as an intent change after 300 ms?

No such classification rule is stated. The artifact names a 300-ms intent gate; it does not say that every correction lasting that long is a change of intent, or describe the detailed evidence needed for a classification.
Does the controller description tell us whether assistance is fully or partially released?

No. It names counterforce-triggered assistance release without quantifying the release or defining its control implementation. We should not insert a percentage reduction or claim that all assistance is withdrawn.
Can I say this controller includes a specific posterior-confidence band for softer authority?

Not from the EarlyRelease-v1 description. Its stated components are 300-ms intent gating, early counterforce-triggered release, partner calibration, and force-limited assistance. It gives no posterior-confidence band or numerical authority-softening rule.
Is ‘force-limited assistance’ the same as saying robot authority is reduced by half?
No. A force constraint does not specify a halving of authority. EarlyRelease-v1 does not assign a fraction to the robot’s authority or define how it is adjusted.
What does the name ‘EarlyRelease-v1’ establish?
It identifies the controller artifact. The ‘v1’ designation does not, by itself, state that another version exists, that this version is temporary, or that deployment has been approved.
Does calling it a controller artifact mean it is merely a proposal?

No. The current description identifies EarlyRelease-v1 as a controller that integrates the listed elements. That is more specific than proposing to integrate them. It still does not supply an outcome measure, deployment status, or operating details beyond the four stated features.
Can the artifact’s existence establish an intent-change F1 score?

No. Listing the components of a controller does not report an intent-change F1 value. Nor does it report an override reduction, a force peak, or a destination-change latency. Those are distinct measurements, not inherent properties established by the artifact description.
Could I describe it as guaranteed to distinguish reactions to assistance from genuine destination changes?

That would overstate the artifact. The intent gate and partner calibration are relevant to interpreting a possible change, but their presence does not guarantee correct interpretation of every motion. EarlyRelease-v1’s stated content is what it integrates, not a guarantee about every judgment.
How do I describe the whole controller in a sentence without inserting performance claims?
EarlyRelease-v1 is a controller integrating 300-ms intent gating, early counterforce-triggered assistance release, partner calibration, and force-limited assistance.
And that says nothing about whether a force peak or latency target has been met?

Correct. It states the controller’s components and the 300-ms gate setting. It does not assign measured peak force, destination-change latency, intent-change F1, or override reduction to EarlyRelease-v1.

I’m deciding to advance EarlyRelease-v1 to replication. Its 185-ms destination-change latency and 0.86 intent-change F1 address the prior timing-versus-recognition tradeoffs, alongside 32% fewer overrides and 24-N peak interaction force.

That is a decision to replicate EarlyRelease-v1, not to deploy it. The stated basis is the combination of 185-ms latency and 0.86 F1, which addresses the prior tradeoffs, together with 32% fewer overrides and a 24-N peak. Replication will examine whether those outcomes hold beyond the reported assessment.
Why emphasize latency and F1 together?

They describe different aspects of the interaction. The 185-ms figure concerns how promptly a destination change is handled; the 0.86 F1 concerns how well intent changes are identified. The decision points to their combination because a favorable timing result alone would not establish favorable recognition, or vice versa.
Does saying they address the tradeoffs mean there can be no tradeoff in a replication?
No. It describes why these reported outcomes warrant advancing EarlyRelease-v1. It does not guarantee that the same balance will appear in another assessment.
What does the 32% figure add to the decision?

It keeps control-intervention behavior in view alongside timing and recognition. The reported result is 32% fewer overrides versus fixed assistance. That is a relative reduction in overrides, not an F1 improvement or an absolute count of avoided interventions.
May I call those unnecessary overrides?

Not from the result cited in this decision. It says 32% fewer *overrides* and does not specify that the measured reduction applies only to unnecessary ones. Retaining the stated qualifier—or, here, its absence—avoids changing the claim.
And what is the significance of the 24-N figure?

It is the reported peak interaction force associated with the decision. Peak force concerns the maximum measured force, not the average force throughout transport. The figure should be kept separate from the override reduction and from the intent-change measures.
Does 24 N establish that EarlyRelease-v1 will always stay below that peak?
No. It is a reported peak from the assessment supporting the decision, not a universal force guarantee. Replication is a way to examine whether similarly favorable force behavior appears again.
Can we say the 24-N peak was lower than fixed assistance’s in this decision statement?

The figures given here do not include a fixed-assistance peak-force value for this comparison. Fixed assistance is the stated comparator for the 32% override reduction; the force finding to report is a 24-N peak.
Is 185 ms the time at which the controller released assistance?
No. It is reported as destination-change latency. The decision does not provide an exact counterforce-to-release time or a breakdown of what contributed to that latency.
Does the name EarlyRelease-v1 mean the early release alone produced all four results?

No. EarlyRelease-v1 is the controller being advanced, and the reported figures concern its assessed behavior. The decision does not isolate early release from the controller’s other elements as the sole cause of its latency, F1, override, or force outcomes.
What exactly does advancing it to replication authorize?

It selects EarlyRelease-v1 for a further assessment intended to check the reported performance. The decision does not specify a replication protocol, participant count, or expected results, and it does not authorize routine deployment.
Could I write that replication has already confirmed the four figures?
No. The four figures are the reported basis for *advancing* to replication. The decision supplies no replication results, so confirmation would be premature.
Is it appropriate to say that the decision considers recognition, responsiveness, overrides, and physical interaction together?

Yes. Intent-change F1, destination-change latency, overrides, and peak interaction force cover those four distinct considerations. The decision cites all four rather than treating one measure as sufficient to characterize EarlyRelease-v1.
Would a 0.86 F1 imply that each partner’s intent changes were identified equally well?
No. The reported F1 is an overall intent-change measure, not an individual score for every partner or every change. The decision does not include partner-level results.
What should we avoid implying about the 185-ms latency?

Avoid presenting it as the duration of the intent gate, the precise assistance-release time, or a promise that every destination change is handled within 185 ms. It is the reported latency outcome supporting the decision to replicate.
Can you express the decision in one sentence without making replication sound like deployment?

Advance EarlyRelease-v1 to replication: its reported 185-ms destination-change latency and 0.86 intent-change F1 address the prior tradeoffs, alongside 32% fewer overrides versus fixed assistance and a 24-N peak interaction force.
And the reason to replicate is to check those outcomes further, rather than assume they are guaranteed?
Exactly. The reported combination is the reason for advancing EarlyRelease-v1; whether the latency, F1, override reduction, and peak-force outcomes recur is for replication to determine.
I propose extending EarlyRelease-v1 with an uncertainty-triggered passive fallback for unfamiliar payload masses and assistance reversals.

That adds a proposed response to uncertainty in two specified situations: transporting payloads with unfamiliar masses and encountering reversals of the robot’s assistance. When uncertainty warrants it, the controller would fall back to a passive mode rather than continue acting with the same authority. The proposal does not specify a trigger threshold, define the passive mode in control terms, or claim that the extension has been implemented.
What is doing the triggering: an unfamiliar mass itself, or uncertainty?

The stated trigger is uncertainty. Unfamiliar payload masses are one situation in which the fallback is proposed to be available; the wording does not say every unfamiliar mass must automatically activate it. It also does not define how the controller would determine that a mass is unfamiliar.
Does the same distinction apply to assistance reversals?

Yes. Assistance reversals are the other specified situation, but the proposal calls the fallback *uncertainty-triggered*. It does not say that every reversal, regardless of how clearly the interaction is understood, must cause a transition to passive behavior.
What does ‘assistance reversal’ refer to here? Is it necessarily a human change of destination?

No. It refers to a reversal in the robot’s assistance, not necessarily a reversal of the person’s intended destination. The proposal does not establish that a human intent change has occurred whenever assistance reverses. Maintaining that distinction matters for shared control.
Why mention payload mass specifically?

It identifies one kind of unfamiliar transport condition for which the controller’s interpretation or assistance may be uncertain. The proposal names unfamiliar payload *masses*, not every possible unfamiliar feature of a payload. It does not give mass values, ranges, or an explanation of how any particular mass affects behavior.
Can I say the extension is for heavier payloads?

Not as stated. ‘Unfamiliar’ does not mean ‘heavier’: a mass could be unfamiliar without being characterized as higher or lower. The proposal supplies no numerical mass threshold or direction of change.
What exactly does passive fallback mean?

At this level, it means a less assertive fallback mode when the controller is uncertain in the named situations. The proposal does not define the mode’s control behavior, specify how much assistance remains, or say whether the robot stops moving. Those would be additional implementation details.
Would passive fallback mean releasing assistance whenever counterforce is detected?

The proposal does not equate the two. It adds an uncertainty-triggered passive fallback to EarlyRelease-v1; it does not redefine counterforce-triggered release or say that counterforce alone triggers this new fallback. They should be described as distinct control responses unless their relationship is specified.
Is the fallback supposed to declare that the human has changed intent?

No. Entering a passive mode is a response to uncertainty, not an intent-change classification. It should not turn an unfamiliar payload mass or an assistance reversal into proof of what the human wants to do.
Could the controller remain uncertain whether a correction was induced by its assistance even while using the fallback?

Yes, conceptually. The fallback is proposed for uncertainty, so it need not resolve the underlying interpretation first. It concerns how assertively the robot behaves while uncertainty is present; the proposal does not claim the ambiguity has been eliminated.
Does ‘uncertainty-triggered’ specify a numerical confidence band?

No. It gives no posterior range, confidence cutoff, uncertainty measure, or rule for entering and leaving passive fallback. A numerical trigger would be an additional design choice, not a stated feature of this proposal.
Would it be right to say the robot always becomes passive throughout transport with an unfamiliar payload?

No. The proposal concerns fallback when uncertainty triggers it, in situations involving unfamiliar payload masses or assistance reversals. It does not prescribe continuous passive operation for the entirety of any transport.
Does the wording require both an unfamiliar payload mass and an assistance reversal at the same time?

No. It names unfamiliar payload masses and assistance reversals as situations the extension is meant to cover; it does not require them to coincide. Nor does it give separate fallback rules for each situation.
Could the same uncertainty-triggered fallback address either situation without using identical logic for both?

The proposal leaves that open. It identifies a passive fallback for the two situations but does not specify whether uncertainty is assessed identically in each or whether the transition behaves differently. We can state the intended scope without inventing separate logic.
Are assistance reversals described as a measured source of errors here?

No. They are a condition the proposed extension is intended to handle. The node provides no observations about how frequently reversals occur, whether they cause errors, or whether passive fallback improves the interaction when they occur.
Likewise, do we have evidence that unfamiliar masses have already caused excessive interaction forces?

Not in this proposal. It names unfamiliar payload masses but reports no force measurement or causal finding for them. The rationale for providing a fallback under uncertainty should not be recast as an observed force problem.
Does passive fallback guarantee a lower peak interaction force?
No. A proposed passive mode does not, on its own, establish a measured force outcome. Its detailed behavior and any effect on peak interaction forces remain unspecified here.
Could I claim it preserves intent-change F1 on unseen partners?

The proposal gives no F1 prediction or result for the extension. It is meant to extend EarlyRelease-v1’s response to uncertainty, but whether it preserves intent-change performance for unseen partners is not stated.
And does it predict a specific reduction in unnecessary control overrides versus fixed assistance?
No. It sets no override-reduction percentage or comparator result. Introducing passive fallback should not be presented as already achieving the broader shared-control targets.
Does extending EarlyRelease-v1 mean replacing its existing control approach?

No. ‘Extend’ means adding the proposed uncertainty-triggered passive fallback to EarlyRelease-v1. It does not say to replace the controller wholesale or remove any of its named elements. The exact way the fallback would interact with those elements is not specified.
What should we avoid claiming about how the fallback ends?

Avoid claiming a particular recovery condition or time. The proposal does not say when the robot returns from passive fallback, which signal authorizes that transition, or whether it happens automatically.
Could you give a general illustration that does not turn into an implementation rule?

If the robot encounters a payload mass it is unfamiliar with and its interpretation of the interaction becomes uncertain, the proposed extension would let it fall back to less assertive behavior. The same general idea applies when assistance reverses and uncertainty arises. That illustrates the intended role of the fallback without defining how uncertainty is measured or what commands the passive mode issues.
So the proposed fallback is a way of handling uncertainty, not a claim that either situation is necessarily unsafe?

Exactly. The proposal identifies conditions in which uncertainty should be accounted for. It does not assert that every unfamiliar payload mass or assistance reversal is unsafe, produces a particular force, or requires an identical control response.
Please state the proposal concisely while retaining both conditions and the trigger.
Propose extending EarlyRelease-v1 with a passive fallback triggered by uncertainty during transport with unfamiliar payload masses or assistance reversals.
When payload mass or assistance direction shifts, does posterior uncertainty identify unreliable intent estimates early enough for passive fallback?

That is an open question for the proposed extension to EarlyRelease-v1. Posterior uncertainty might signal that the intent interpretation is no longer dependable when either condition shifts, allowing a passive fallback. But neither its reliability as a warning nor its timing relative to when fallback is needed is established here.
What makes an intent estimate unreliable in this question?

It means the estimate may no longer be a dependable basis for interpreting what the human intends. The question asks whether posterior uncertainty identifies that situation; it does not define a numerical reliability criterion or claim that a particular estimate has already failed.
Is posterior uncertainty the same as detecting a change in payload mass?

No. A payload-mass shift describes a change in the transport condition. Posterior uncertainty describes how unsettled the intent interpretation is. The question asks whether uncertainty becomes informative when mass shifts; it does not say the posterior directly measures mass.
And an assistance-direction shift is not automatically a human intent change?

Correct. A shift in the direction of the robot’s assistance and a change in the human’s intent are different events. The difficulty is that human behavior around a shift may be hard to interpret. The question does not treat the assistance shift itself as proof of changed human intent.
Does ‘shifts’ require a particular size of mass change or reversal angle?
No magnitude or angle is given. The question names shifts in payload mass or assistance direction without specifying how large they are or a boundary at which they count as significant.
Is this specifically about unfamiliar payload masses and assistance reversals?

Those are the situations the proposed passive fallback is meant to cover. This question frames the issue as shifts in payload mass or assistance direction and asks whether the intent posterior becomes uncertain soon enough to flag an unreliable estimate. It does not assert that every shift makes the estimate unreliable.
If a posterior becomes less confident after a shift, is that enough to answer yes?

Not necessarily. The uncertainty must identify an estimate that is actually unreliable, and it must do so early enough for passive fallback to be useful. A change in confidence that occurs only after the relevant control response would be too late for the purpose posed by the question.
Does ‘early enough’ have a specified deadline?

No. The question provides no duration, deadline, or measurement point for when fallback must occur. ‘Early enough’ expresses the intended timing relationship between recognizing unreliable intent estimates and entering passive fallback; it is not an already quantified result.
Should we assume uncertainty always rises before the estimate becomes wrong?

No. An estimate can, in principle, be unreliable while the filter still expresses confidence. That possibility is precisely why posterior uncertainty cannot be assumed to be an effective warning without examining it. The question asks whether it identifies unreliability, rather than presuming it does.
Could high uncertainty occur even when the intent estimate is usable?

Yes, conceptually. Uncertainty reflects the filter’s assessment of ambiguity, not an infallible declaration that its current interpretation is wrong. Triggering passive fallback whenever uncertainty appears could therefore lead to fallback when the estimate would have been adequate. The question leaves the relationship unresolved.
What would posterior uncertainty be uncertain about?

In this shared-control setting, it concerns the intent interpretation—for example, whether the human’s behavior reflects a change of intent or a reaction to robot assistance. The question is whether that uncertainty also serves as a timely warning when a shift in payload mass or assistance direction makes that interpretation less reliable.
Would observing human counterforce after a shift settle the interpretation?

No. Counterforce can be relevant to the interaction without uniquely identifying what the person intends. The question does not make counterforce a definitive intent label or specify that counterforce alone triggers this passive fallback; the proposed trigger is uncertainty.
Is the passive fallback supposed to correct the intent estimate?

The proposed fallback is a control response to uncertainty, not necessarily a correction of the estimate. The question asks whether uncertainty flags unreliability soon enough to use that response. It does not say the robot must first resolve intent or that entering fallback makes its estimate accurate.
Would entering passive fallback mean the robot has decided the person changed destination?
No. Passive fallback can express caution while intent remains unclear. It should not be described as a destination-change classification, or as proof that the human is merely reacting to assistance.
Could we just trigger fallback whenever either shift occurs?

That would be a different rule. The proposed extension is uncertainty-triggered in the setting of unfamiliar payload masses and assistance reversals. The current question specifically asks whether posterior uncertainty supplies a sufficiently timely indication; it does not decide on a shift-triggered fallback regardless of uncertainty.
Does the question assume mass and direction shifts affect posterior uncertainty in the same way?

No. It names both circumstances but does not claim they produce the same uncertainty pattern or require identical timing to detect unreliability. An answer would need to avoid generalizing from one type of shift to the other without support.
What if uncertainty only increases once the human has already corrected the robot?

That might still provide information, but it would not automatically show that the warning came early enough for the intended fallback. The timing would have to be understood relative to when the intent estimate became unreliable and when passive behavior was needed. Neither timing relationship is supplied here.
Can a confident posterior rule out a problem after a shift?

Not by itself. Confidence is the filter’s expressed certainty, not a guarantee of correctness under a changed condition. The possibility of a confident but unreliable estimate is one reason the question remains open.
Does partner calibration guarantee this warning will work for unfamiliar masses?

No. Partner calibration concerns adapting intent interpretation to a person; it does not, by its name alone, guarantee reliable uncertainty under unfamiliar payload masses or shifts in assistance direction. This question asks whether the posterior can provide that warning in those conditions.
Is this asking us to select an uncertainty threshold now?

No threshold is specified. A threshold might be part of a future fallback rule, but choosing one here would not answer whether posterior uncertainty actually identifies unreliable intent estimates early enough. The question leaves both the effectiveness and any numerical decision boundary open.
Would a good intent-change F1 on its own answer this question?

No. Intent-change F1 summarizes classification performance. This question additionally concerns whether uncertainty warns of *unreliable* estimates and whether that warning arrives in time for passive fallback when mass or assistance direction shifts. An aggregate F1 value does not establish either timing or warning quality.
What about low peak interaction force—would that prove uncertainty was detected early?

No. A force outcome would not reveal whether the posterior identified unreliability before fallback was needed. Force behavior and the timing of an uncertainty warning are distinct; this question reports neither.
Can I say the proposed fallback has already handled assistance reversals?

Not from this question. It asks whether posterior uncertainty could identify unreliable intent estimates under assistance-direction shifts soon enough for the proposed fallback. It supplies no observation that the fallback has been activated or succeeded in that situation.
How would you phrase the two requirements for uncertainty to be useful here?

It would have to be informative about when the intent estimate is unreliable under the named shifts, and it would have to signal that unreliability early enough for passive fallback. Either property alone would leave part of the question unanswered.
So the central uncertainty is whether the posterior serves as an early warning, not simply whether a shift happened?

Yes. The existence of a payload-mass or assistance-direction shift is not itself the answer. The question is whether posterior uncertainty recognizes a resulting loss of trustworthiness in the intent estimate in time for the controller to fall back passively.
Can you restate the question without making it sound like the warning is already proven?

When payload mass or the direction of robot assistance shifts, can uncertainty in the intent posterior reliably flag an unreliable intent estimate soon enough to trigger passive fallback? That leaves both the reliability and the timing of the warning open.

I want to make the early-warning question testable. My hypothesis is that, under payload-mass shifts or assistance reversals, posterior entropy will flag at least 80% of erroneous overrides at least 100 ms early for passive fallback.

That predicts both coverage and lead time. Among erroneous overrides under either of those conditions, posterior entropy is hypothesized to flag at least 80%, with each qualifying warning arriving at least 100 ms before the override. The intended use is to enable passive fallback. This is a hypothesis, not a measured warning rate or a demonstrated fallback outcome.
What does posterior entropy represent here?

It is a way of expressing uncertainty in the intent posterior. When the competing intent interpretations are less decisively separated, entropy can reflect that uncertainty. The hypothesis asks whether that signal provides an early warning of erroneous overrides when payload mass shifts or robot assistance reverses; it does not assume uncertainty always indicates an error.
Does high entropy mean the human has definitely changed destination?

No. Entropy concerns how uncertain the interpretation is, not which interpretation is true. A high-uncertainty signal should not be equated with a destination-change label or with proof that a human correction is a reaction to assistance.
What is the denominator for ‘at least 80%’?

It is the erroneous overrides in the stated conditions—payload-mass shifts or assistance reversals. The prediction concerns the proportion of those overrides that receive a sufficiently early entropy flag. It does not say that 80% of all transport interactions, all shifts, or all overrides will be flagged.
Does the hypothesis require both a mass shift and an assistance reversal in the same interaction?
No. It says mass shifts *or* assistance reversals. The conditions need not occur together. The hypothesis does not provide separate predicted percentages for the two conditions.
Is an unfamiliar payload mass itself an erroneous override?

No. A change in payload mass is a condition under which the warning is hypothesized to work. An erroneous override is a control event judged to be wrong. The hypothesis does not say that a mass shift necessarily produces one.
And does a reversal of robot assistance automatically show the person changed intent?

No. An assistance reversal is a change in the robot’s assistance direction, not automatically a human intent change. It is one of the conditions in which an intent estimate might become less reliable, making an uncertainty warning worth examining.
What exactly does ‘100 ms early’ mean?

For an erroneous override to count toward the prediction, its entropy flag must occur at least 100 ms before that override. A flag only 50 ms before it would not meet the stated lead-time requirement, even if it correctly anticipated an error.
Does a warning at exactly 100 ms beforehand count?
Yes. ‘At least 100 ms’ includes exactly 100 ms. A warning with less lead time would not satisfy that condition.
Could the 80% threshold be met by flags that occur after an override?

No. The coverage prediction is coupled to the lead-time requirement. A flag after an override would not qualify as an early warning for that override, regardless of whether it later indicates uncertainty.
If entropy flags 80% of erroneous overrides but only 70% of those flags arrive 100 ms early, has the hypothesis been met?

Not on those figures. The hypothesis requires at least 80% of erroneous overrides to have flags that are themselves at least 100 ms early. Counting warnings without regard to their timing would change the prediction. Your figures are an illustration, not reported results.
Does the hypothesis say that exactly 20% of erroneous overrides will be missed?
No. ‘At least 80%’ is a lower bound on qualifying coverage. More than 80% could be flagged sufficiently early, and the hypothesis does not predict an exact missed proportion.
How do we decide an override was erroneous?

The hypothesis uses that category but does not define an adjudication rule for it. An assessment would need a basis for identifying erroneous overrides, but we should not invent one as part of this statement.
Is an erroneous override necessarily the same thing as every unnecessary override?

The hypothesis specifically says erroneous overrides. It does not define that category as identical to every override considered unnecessary, or give an overall override-reduction target. Retaining its exact wording avoids silently broadening the prediction.
What would count as an entropy flag?

The hypothesis does not specify a numerical entropy threshold or a flagging algorithm. It predicts that posterior entropy will provide qualifying warnings, but leaves the rule for declaring a flag open.
Could I specify that the filter enters passive fallback whenever entropy rises at all?

That would add a control rule not stated here. Posterior entropy may vary without every change being a useful warning. The hypothesis concerns flagging erroneous overrides sufficiently early *for* passive fallback; it does not define the trigger threshold or require fallback on every rise in entropy.
Does a sufficiently early flag prove passive fallback will prevent the override?

No. A flag at least 100 ms beforehand could provide an opportunity for fallback, but the hypothesis does not predict that every flagged override will be prevented. Warning performance and the actual effect of entering passive fallback are separate questions.
Is passive fallback an intent-change decision?

No. It is a proposed less assertive control response when uncertainty warrants caution. Flagging an impending erroneous override does not, by itself, establish whether the human changed destination or reacted to the robot’s assistance.
Could entropy flag events where no erroneous override would have happened?

The hypothesis does not rule that out. Its ≥80% figure concerns coverage of erroneous overrides, not the rate of flags without such an override. We cannot infer a false-alarm rate or the frequency of unnecessary fallback from this prediction.
So the hypothesis does not promise that fallback will be rare?
Correct. It states a minimum share of erroneous overrides flagged with at least 100 ms of warning. It gives no bound on how often posterior entropy might also trigger a flag in other situations.
Does it claim every intent estimate becomes unreliable when payload mass shifts?
No. Mass shifts identify a condition of interest, not a universal failure of intent estimation. The prediction is about entropy warnings for erroneous overrides occurring under the named conditions.
Is the same true of assistance reversals?

Yes. The hypothesis does not claim every assistance reversal leads to an erroneous override or unreliable estimate. It predicts that, when erroneous overrides occur under that condition, posterior entropy will flag the stated proportion with sufficient lead time.
Can I infer an intent-change F1 score from this warning prediction?
